## Architectural Style & Fit

**Actual style**: modular monolith with a clean, acyclic internal layering; single-process desktop application; no distribution. Hybrid influence: services+adapters at the Tauri edge (`docs/architecture/adrs/ADR-004`), event bus + jobs in storage (`ADR-005`).

**Why it fits**: the product is single-user, local-process, CPU-bound on parsing, with a hard isolation requirement for untrusted input. A modular monolith gives transactional integrity, in-process latency, one deployment artefact, and zero network failure modes — each of which is a *requirement*, not a shortcut.
**Cost it introduces**: the process is a single failure domain (acceptable: a crash is a crash for a desktop app) and the frontend and native core share a repo/release cadence (acceptable: one product).
**Unnecessary complexity currently paid**:
- Three placeholder crates/features with no consumer (`luma-sync`, `luma-ai`, the device/platform UI surfaces) — a maintenance and *credibility* cost, not a runtime cost.
- A test-only bridge binary living in the shipped crate tree, with a frontend transport and an env-var branch for it — real complexity carried permanently for a test harness.
- A dual-mode API client (real + mock + localStorage) as one class rather than a seam — complexity that now taxes every one of 109 methods.

## Module / Domain Boundaries

Boundaries are derived from **business capability** and they hold: Library | Import | Reader | Annotation | Bookmark | Collection/Tag | Search | Progress/Session | Knowledge (notes/flashcards/research) | Backup | Maintenance | Diagnostics | Settings. `crates/luma-storage/src/services/*` maps 1:1 to this list (13 services), and `commands/*` mirrors it (16 modules).

**Deviation found**: `reader_service.rs` (622 L) hosts three session models (reflowable / PDF page / canonical) with three bounded-cache maps and duplicated bounded-insert logic (prior audit's inline-duplication note still verified). Cohesion is acceptable; the duplication is the smell.
**No god *native* module** was found beyond that; `knowledge_repo.rs` (789 L) and `epub_doc.rs` (844 L) are cohesive.
**Frontend deviation**: the boundary scheme stops at the folder level — no enforced feature isolation, and a single component composes six features.

## Service & Boundary Extraction

**No extraction is warranted.** There is no scaling divergence, no team ownership split, no independent deployment need, no fault-isolation requirement, no separate data ownership, and no differing release cadence. Extracting services would add network failure modes, observability burden, and consistency work in exchange for nothing. **Explicitly not-justified change.** If a cloud sync capability is ever built, `luma-sync` is the pre-identified seam (per the prior audit's watchlist) and should remain a crate boundary, not a service.

## Dependency Graph

Verified acyclic and enforced (see PART II). Upward dependencies: none. Infrastructure leakage into the domain: none found — `luma-core` depends on nothing, `luma-security` depends only on `luma-core`, and no domain crate depends on the Tauri layer. Shared mutable state across boundaries: the storage `Database`/`CacheManager` handles (intentional, process-global).

## API / Contract Architecture

- **Boundary**: Tauri commands — typed arguments, typed `LumaError`, ~109 commands, documented in `docs/reference/TAURI-IPC-API.md` (docs claim 33; the actual client exposes far more — a documentation-drift finding).
- **Compatibility strategy**: none needed (single in-repo consumer, versioned together) — correct at this maturity.
- **Weakness**: no machine-readable command registry shared between Rust and TS, so the two sides can drift and only fail at runtime (CQ-MED-NEW3). This is the one contract-architecture improvement with real payoff.
- **Business logic at the edge**: not found — command modules are thin adapters over services. ✅

## Sync / Async, Event-Driven, CQRS, Event Sourcing

- **Sync/async**: commands are async over IPC; the UI is promise-based. Storage uses `spawn_blocking`-style separation for CPU work. Appropriate.
- **Events**: `luma-storage/src/events` defines a typed domain event bus (ADR-005) with job-progress events bridged to the frontend via `onDomainEvent` (`luma://job/progress`, `luma://library/book-imported`, …). This is a **local pub/sub for progress reporting**, not distributed messaging — proportionate and correctly scoped. Verified caveat: `onDomainEvent` returns a **no-op unlisten** on failure and logs only, so an event-loss is invisible to callers.
- **CQRS**: absent. ✅ Correctly not introduced for a local CRUD app.
- **Event sourcing**: absent. ✅ Correctly not introduced — SQLite tables + a `sync` version column (`version`, `device_id`, `is_deleted`, `updated_at`) provide the change metadata needed later without the cost.

## Data Ownership & Consistency

- Ownership is aligned with boundaries: `Book` vs `BookFile` separation (ADR-0011), annotations owned by the logical book, `sync` metadata on every mutable entity.
- Single-writer discipline: one write connection, WAL, FK cascades, transactional multi-entity mutations (delete-with-artifacts, backup restore). **Correct consistency model chosen (strong, local) and not downgraded for fashion.**
- **Frontend-side consistency gap** (ARCH-MED-2): progress is persisted through a 400 ms debounce held in a factory closure, and `closeReader` flushes **only if a timer is still pending**; there is no `beforeunload`/visibility flush. So the last position can be lost when the timer has already fired (the common case for a reader left open) → on reopen, the user lands on a slightly stale position. Small but user-visible, and it directly touches the product's promise of remembering where you were. Also note: a *stale-locator* consequence — the reader resumes from `initial_progress` and reparses CFI by regex (CQ-MED-NEW2), so this interacts with the locator mini-language.

## Availability / Reliability / Scalability

- Reliability mechanisms present: WAL, FK enforcement, transactional backup/restore, job cancellation, bounded caches, resource guards. Mechanism *absent*: any retry/idempotency thinking for the *file system* (an imported file removed externally is handled by `reconcile`), and any crash-recovery path for the UI (FE-CRIT-1).
- Scaling: **not a requirement**; correctly not engineered. The only scaling dimension that matters is *library size on one machine*, which is addressed in Rust (FTS5, indexes, bounded caches) and **not** in the frontend (fake pagination + no virtualization) — that asymmetry is the honest summary of where performance work remains.

## Caching & Storage

- Storage choice is correct: SQLite + FTS5 for relational + full-text on a single-user local dataset; filesystem for documents; LRU `Arc<CanonicalDocument>` for parsed trees. No document/KV/graph store is needed. **No change.**
- Caching layers: HTTP/CDN cache is irrelevant (no network); canonical-document LRU is the right client-adjacent cache; the frontend correctly has none.
- Invalidation: `rebuild_search_index`, `reconcile_files`, `cleanup_caches`, `vacuum_database` maintenance commands exist and are exposed in Settings ✅.

## Security Architecture

**Verified strong (preserve)**: trust boundary at IPC with a minimal capability set (`core:default` only — no filesystem/shell/http plugin permissions granted); path-traversal guards with canonicalization; archive-bomb limits; content hashing for identity; an **active ammonia-based sanitizer** applied to every untrusted HTML/metadata path (`epub_doc.rs`, `cbz_doc.rs`, `extractors/*`, `html_doc`, `markdown_doc`) with `class`/`id`/`title`/`lang` as the only generic attributes; typed errors rather than panics in the command layer.

### ARCH-MED-3 — CSP is weaker than the threat model requires, and permissive in the wrong direction

`app.security.csp = "default-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data: asset: https:"`

- `'unsafe-inline'` under `default-src` covers **script-src**, so if the sanitizer ever misses an inline script or an `onerror`-style handler, CSP provides **no** second line of defence. For an app whose entire input is untrusted third-party HTML, defence-in-depth here is not optional. (`style-src` inline is needed for the injected chapter markup — the fix is to split the policy: allow `'unsafe-inline'` for **styles only**, never for scripts.)
- No `object-src 'none'`, no `base-uri 'self'`, no `frame-ancestors 'none'`, no `form-action 'none'`, no `connect-src` — each is a cheap, standard hardening step, and `frame-ancestors` matters because the app renders untrusted content.
- **`img-src … https:` actively permits remote loads from sanitized EPUB content.** Any `<img src="https://…">` in a book will be fetched — a tracking-pixel / IP-and-timing leak from a product whose headline promise is "local-first & private". The sanitizer's default allowlist keeps `img`, and the CSP then allows the fetch. This is the one place where the privacy *principle* is not backed by the *mechanism*.
**Direction**: pin `script-src 'self'` (Tauri injects its IPC with the necessary hashes/nonces); `img-src 'self' data: asset:` (drop `https:`, or rewrite remote image URLs to a placeholder at the sanitizer boundary and surface a "remote content blocked" affordance); add `object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; form-action 'none'`. Then self-host fonts (FE-MED-2) so the policy needs no third-party origin at all.
**Validation**: a fixture EPUB with a remote image + an inline `onerror` handler; assert no outbound request and no execution. **Priority**: 🟠 HIGH. **Complexity**: Low config + one sanitizer-policy decision.

### ARCH-MED-4 — Dev/test bridge: unauthenticated loopback API over the user's library

`apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/bin/browser_reader_bridge.rs` is a cargo binary that binds `127.0.0.1:0`, opens the real SQLite database, imports fixtures, and serves commands over plain HTTP with **no authentication token**; the frontend's `BrowserIntegrationTransport` will talk to it whenever `VITE_LUMA_BROWSER_INTEGRATION_TEST === "true"`. It sets **no CORS headers** (so a browser page on another origin cannot *read* responses — good), but **any local process/user on the machine can read and mutate the library while it runs**, and the crate tree ships it next to the app.
**Assessment**: proportionate as *test tooling*; the risk is entirely about it becoming reachable in a build a user runs. **Direction**: keep it (it is genuinely useful for the reader harness), but make its containment explicit — a feature flag that is off by default, a `#[cfg]`-gated binary target excluded from `bundle`, a hard-coded loopback-only bind with a per-run token echoed to the test process, and a line in the threat model stating it exists. **Priority**: 🟡 Medium (contextual).

## Multi-Tenancy / Edge / Gateway

N/A (single-user local application) — and no multi-tenancy abstraction was invented where none is needed. ✅

## Configuration, Deployment, Cloud / Serverless / Containers / Kubernetes

- Configuration: Tauri conf + capability file + env vars for the test transport + `deny.toml`. No secrets in the repo. Feature flags: none real. `MockDataStore` acts as an implicit always-on fallback, which is a *configuration* concern worth naming (ARCH-MED-5).
- Deployment: desktop bundling (`targets: "all"`), no cloud infrastructure at all — the cheapest possible architecture for these requirements.
- Serverless/containers/Kubernetes: **N/A and correctly absent.** Recommend recording this as an ADR (see roadmap) so it is not re-litigated.
- **ARCH-MED-5**: release artefacts are built with `minify: "esbuild"` and **`sourcemap` only when `TAURI_DEBUG`**, so there is no way to symbolicate a field crash. Combined with no error reporting, a shipped defect is unattributable. Cheap, high-value fix; pairs with FE-CRIT-1.

## Real-Time

Job progress via the local event bus is the real-time requirement, and it is implemented with the simplest mechanism that satisfies it. **No WebSockets/SSE needed.** ✅ Correct.

## AI / ML / LLM / Agents

`luma-ai` (172 L) defines traits with **no implementations and zero consumers**; no model, prompt, RAG, vector store, or agent code exists. **Do not build agent/tool infrastructure now.** The architectural advice is therefore: leave the crate frozen (it costs nothing), and when a real feature arrives, define the seam at the *service* level (`luma-storage/src/services/`) invoking an `luma-ai` trait, not in the frontend — and keep inference out of the UI thread. If an LLM feature ever ships, the privacy promise becomes the dominant architectural constraint (local model or explicit opt-in per document), and that decision deserves an ADR before code.

## Frontend / Backend Architecture

Covered in PART I. The load-bearing conclusion: **the split is correct (systems logic in Rust, presentation in TS) and the frontend is thin** — it holds little logic and (critically) no shadow copy of server state. The two frontend structural gaps (navigation ownership, failure representation) are the architectural work that remains.

## Team Topology / Conway's Law

Solo maintainer, single repository, single deployment artefact — and the architecture matches it exactly (modular monolith, no service boundaries to coordinate, one release train). This is *correct* alignment, not a compromise. **Watchlist trigger**: if a second engineer is added, the first thing that will break is `LibraryView` and `tauri.ts`, because both are the only files every frontend change touches — i.e. guaranteed merge conflicts. Fixing CQ-01/CQ-03 *before* the second contributor arrives is the cheapest possible sequence.

## Developer Experience

- **Strong**: one-command gates (`pnpm ci:checks`), fast frontend test suite (5 s), the transport seam letting the whole UI run in a browser with mocks, an extremely rich docs set, and audit reports that trace debt IDs to commits.
- **Friction found**: (1) the test suite dirties the tree (CQ-CRIT-1); (2) the browser mock mode is *not* what the docs describe — the docs promise "rapid UI iteration" in the browser, but in the browser the app renders the **Google-Fonts-styled** layout while the shipped app renders fallback fonts (FE-MED-2), so browser iteration can produce layouts that do not match production; (3) two copy-pasted verifier scripts make it unclear which one is authoritative; (4) `docs/audits/*` and `docs/*-REPORT.md` overlap heavily (about 20 report files), making "what is the current state?" a search problem — the audit trail is a strength that is becoming a liability.

## Cost / TCO / Vendor Lock-In

Zero infrastructure cost, zero vendor lock-in, no managed services — an unusually low TCO for this capability set. The only third-party *runtime* dependency is the font CDN (removable, and removing it also fixes a privacy and offline issue). Tauri/SQLite/pdfjs/ammonia are all open and portable. **No cost action required beyond FE-MED-2.**

## ADRs / Architecture Documentation / Fitness Functions

- ADRs: 24 + 5 in `docs/architecture/adrs/`, covering exactly the right decisions (Book vs BookFile, ingestion/dedup, session architecture, EPUB/PDF rendering, typed IPC, dependency policy, DB concurrency, modular boundaries). This is exemplary.
- **Drift found** (documentation is the source of truth for the next engineer, so this matters): docs claim **React 19** (actual: 18.3.1), **`TypeScript 5.6`** in a badge while the app pins `^5.6.0` (fine) but `@types/node ^22` vs root `^22` (fine), **33 IPC commands** (the client exposes ~109), `@luma/ui` exporting `Card`/`Modal` and `library-ui` exporting `BookListItem` (neither exists), `luma-ai`/`luma-sync` described as integrations (both unused), and `docs/reference/CRATES.md`/`FRONTEND-ARCHITECTURE.md` describing a directory layout that omits six of the ten existing feature folders.
- Fitness functions: **Rust ✅ (new, passing)**; frontend ❌; a11y ❌; bundle size ❌.
- **Recommendation**: add a "documentation drift" check to CI for the cheap-to-verify claims (React version from `package.json`, package exports vs docs) or, more simply, add a `docs/architecture/CURRENT-STATE.md` that is *the* answered question "what is actually in this repo today", and make the audit reports append-only history. Also: **consolidate the ADR pair-files** (`ADR-0001-to-0005.md`, `ADR-0006-to-0010.md` alongside the individual files) — currently the same decisions exist in two places and can diverge.

## Evolution / Migration / Rewrite Assessment

- **Evolution path is clear and incremental**: keep the modular monolith; fix frontend state ownership; add the missing test tier; harden CSP; self-host fonts. None of this requires a migration strategy, since none of it crosses a boundary.
- **Trigger watchlist** (do NOT act until a trigger fires): `luma-sync` unfreezes when real multi-device sync is a product decision (then: CRDT/version-vector design + an ADR + conflict UX, in that order); `luma-ai` unfreezes on a shipped LLM feature (privacy-first ADR first); `luma-storage` splits only if a second binary must ship without SQLite (no such requirement today).
- **Rewrite assessment**: **not justified anywhere.** Every problem found is localized and testable (`tauri.ts` has a seam; `LibraryView` needs tests first but is decomposable; theme consolidation is mechanical; CSP is config). A rewrite would destroy the enforced layering and the reader invariants that are the project's genuine moat. Recommend an explicit ADR stating "no rewrite; incremental remediation only", so the decision is not re-litigated under fatigue.

## Trade-off Ledger (principal decisions, as they should have been recorded)

```text
Decision: Modular monolith (Rust workspace) + single-window Tauri shell
Requirement: local-first privacy, in-process latency, untrusted-input isolation
Options: monolith | modular monolith | microservices | serverless
Benefits: transactional integrity, zero network failure modes, one artefact, lowest TCO
Costs: single process failure domain; coupled release cadence (acceptable: one product)
Decision: KEEP — and record as an ADR so it is not re-litigated

Decision: Hand-written, transport-injectable IPC client instead of a data-fetching framework
Requirement: testable UI without a native runtime; no duplicated server state
Benefits: zero client cache to invalidate; whole UI runs in a browser against mocks
Costs: 109 methods + inline mock branches in one file; no request dedup/cancellation
Decision: KEEP the seam, SPLIT the module (transport vs domains vs mock), add per-request sequencing

Decision: CSR only, single bundle
Requirement: desktop shell, offline, no SEO, no personalization needs
Benefits: simplest possible rendering model
Costs: one 948 kB chunk pays for features the user may never open
Decision: KEEP CSR; ADD lazy feature/engine chunks + a bundle budget

Decision: Three theme/token systems + 135 literals
Requirement: (none — this is drift, not a decision)
Decision: CONSOLIDATE to one; this is the clearest case of accidental complexity in the frontend

Decision: Durable state in SQLite; theme in localStorage
Requirement: "own your data"; zero-durable-localStorage invariant
Benefits: complete backup surface; a documented, narrow exception
Costs: two persistence mechanisms with two authorities for one user-visible setting
Decision: KEEP the exception but give theme exactly ONE writer (an IPC-backed settings row would be cleaner)

Decision: No a11y quality attribute stated
Requirement: (missing)
Consequence: a11y is absent by construction in 14 interactive files
Decision: ADD the requirement, then treat the fixes as the first delivery against it

Decision: Rewrite the frontend?
Evidence: every gap is localized and testable
Decision: NOT JUSTIFIED — incremental remediation only
```

# STRENGTHS WORTH PRESERVING (do not "modernize" these away)

1. **The enforced, acyclic Rust layering with a fitness test that fails on policy escape** — the single best artefact in the repo. Extend the pattern to the frontend; never weaken it.
2. **No duplicated server state in the client.** Resist every future temptation to add a global cache of IPC data.
3. **The transport/DI seam** that lets the entire UI be tested without a native runtime — finish it instead of replacing it.
4. **The Rust-side untrusted-input boundary** (path guards, bomb limits, hashing, ammonia sanitization with explicit `class/id/title/lang` policy) — the security foundation the CSP should now match.
5. **Correct consistency, storage, and rendering choices for the requirements** (SQLite WAL/strong-local; CSR/offline; no CQRS/event-sourcing/SSR).
6. **Why-oriented comments and rationale-rich code** (security trade-offs, PDF gating, sanitizer contracts).
7. **Domain vocabulary discipline** (`spine`, `anchor`, `canonical`, `Book` vs `BookFile`) and typed IDs over primitives.
8. **Small, scoped, audit-traceable commits** and a documentation culture that is rare at this stage.
9. **Restraint**: no premature abstraction, no SOLID cargo-culting, no fashion-driven architecture. This is a *quality* to defend, not a gap to fill.

# ANSWERS TO THE MISSION QUESTIONS

**Frontend — is it predictable, maintainable, accessible, performant, secure, testable, evolvable?**
Predictable: mostly, except theme (4 writers) and navigation (state death on unmount). Maintainable: yes for a small team, with two concentrate-all-change files. Accessible: **no** — this is the largest unaddressed quality gap. Performant: acceptable at small scale, unmeasured and structurally exposed at large library size. Secure: strong mechanisms, weak CSP perimeter. Testable: the seam exists but the test tier for components does not. Evolvable: yes — every problem found is localized.

**Does every piece of state have the correct owner?** No. Server state ownership is *correct and better than typical*. Durable state ownership is correct. But navigation state is owned by a component with a shorter lifetime than the state, theme has four writers, and the reader store holds local UI toggles it does not need.

**Are boundaries preventing cascading change?** Native: yes, and enforced. Frontend: no — no enforced feature isolation, and one component composes six features, so library changes cascade into unrelated features.

**Is rendering strategy appropriate?** Yes (CSR/offline for a desktop shell). The *delivery* of that strategy (one eager bundle) is not.

**Can the interface remain usable under failure/poor network?** Network: yes (local-first, no network in the data path — except fonts and remote images, which is exactly backwards). Failure: no — failures are silent and any render error kills the window.

**Can keyboard/AT users operate critical workflows?** Partially. The reader has real shortcuts and some ARIA, but 14 interactive files have no a11y affordances at all, dialogs lack semantics/traps, focus visibility likely fails 3:1, and global `user-select: none` blocks copying the user's own content.

**Can real-user performance be measured and protected from regression?** No. There is no field capture, no bundle budget, no CI frontend gate, and the one committed perf artefact is overwritten by running the tests.

**Are frontend security boundaries enforced correctly?** Mechanisms: yes (sanitizer at the Rust boundary, minimal capabilities, path guards). Perimeter: not yet — inline scripts permitted at the CSP level, remote images permitted, fonts fetched from a third party.

**Which architecture should be preserved, improved, simplified, or rejected?** *Preserve* the modular monolith, the crate layering and its fitness tests, the local-only consistency model, and the transport seam. *Improve*: frontend navigation/state ownership, the failure/observability tier, CSP, a11y, the test tier. *Simplify*: one theme/token system, the API client's mock duality, the dead configuration surface, the one eager bundle. *Reject*: services, brokers, CQRS/event sourcing, SSR/meta-frameworks, a client server-state cache, a design-system rebuild, i18n-for-its-own-sake, and any rewrite.

**Is this codebase easy to understand and safely change?** Yes — more so than most codebases of this size, and the reason is discipline (enforced layering, typed errors, rationale comments, small commits) rather than tooling. The two places where that property breaks down are `lib/tauri.ts` and `features/library/LibraryView.tsx`, both of which every frontend change must touch, and both of which are fixable in days with the test tier in place.

**Is complexity essential or accidental?** Essential: format parsing, anchoring, text-layer geometry, migrations, the security sanitizer — all localized, documented, and protected by tests. Accidental: the god module/component, three theme systems, 109 inline mock branches, dead configuration surfaces, fabrications in `BookTable`, and a decorative pagination control.

**Which duplication is dangerous?** `ReadingProgress` construction ×4 (changes together), the locator mini-language re-parsed in 5 places, the two divergent verifier scripts, and the split theme/token knowledge. Incidental duplication (six document engines, per-package tsconfigs) should deliberately remain.

**Which technical debt has real interest?** The god module/component (every frontend change pays twice — and will pay in merge conflicts the day a second engineer joins), the non-hermetic test, the theme scatter, and the missing failure/observability tier.

**Can legacy be improved incrementally?** There is no legacy to modernize — only four localized hotspots with existing seams. Do it incrementally, in the order above, with the new test tier carrying each change.
